title: Random forests identify surface geometry relationships associated with reduced bacterial attachment
summary: A screen of 2176 polymer surface patterns supplied measurements for random-forest models linking geometry to bacterial attachment. Held-out topographies supported predictive associations between attachment and surface coverage, feature size and spacing; the models outperformed a simpler roughness descriptor. The anti-attachment hits themselves came from experimental screening, not AI selection. The AI contribution is a learned structure–response relationship; the separate biological mechanism and animal findings are not attributed to AI.
organization: University of Nottingham; Maastricht University; Eindhoven University of Technology; La Trobe University

evidence.tested: Random-forest models trained on 70% of measured surface-attachment data and evaluated on 30% across 50 resamples; source-reported test R² values were 0.851 and 0.810 for the two modeled bacterial species. A simpler roughness descriptor performed less well.
evidence.unknown: No newly fabricated AI-selected surface was tested as a prospective design prediction. The experimental screen selected the best surfaces. Mechanistic and animal experiments are not represented as AI-enabled findings, and clinical device benefit remains unestablished.
evidence.ai_role: Random forests learned geometry-to-attachment mappings from 68 topographical descriptors; SHAP identified influential geometric variables and conditional design relationships beyond a single roughness descriptor.

source_review.scope: Exact primary article-front identity/date; full relevant surface-screening, learned-model Methods and result paragraphs; fresh PubMed publication-status relationships. Only the material geometry/attachment association is represented.
